issues.title: Step-up authentication has no carrier at the token endpoint
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
A PDP that denies because the subject authenticated too weakly knows something
the client could act on: which `acr` and `amr` values would have permitted the
request. Neither end of that is specified today.

- AuthZEN carries `acr_values` / `amr_values` only in the **non-normative
  example** of Section 5.5.2.3. The keys are never defined, so there is
  nothing normative for this profile to reference.
- `insufficient_user_authentication` (RFC 9470) is defined for resource
  servers. The token endpoint has no equivalent.

The Error Mapping section currently says an AS SHOULD surface the requirement
and declines to define how.

Closing this needs work in both specifications, which is why it may deserve
its own document rather than a paragraph here. The AuthZEN half should be
raised with the AuthZEN WG.

issues.title: No error code is named for a policy denial
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
The Error Mapping table says "fail the request; do not issue" for a gate
denial without naming an OAuth error code. That reflects the state of the
neighbouring specifications, which have no consensus:

- **RFC 8693** Section 2.2.1 says the AS MUST use `invalid_request` when a
  token is "unacceptable based on policy" - which contradicts RFC 6749
  Section 5.2, where `invalid_request` means the request is *malformed*.
- **Identity chaining** defers to RFC 7523 Section 3.1, i.e. `invalid_grant`.
- **ID-JAG** and **Transaction Tokens** describe policy denial in detail and
  name no error code at all.
- `access_denied` is semantically exact ("the resource owner or authorization
  server denied the request") but is defined at the authorization endpoint in
  RFC 6749 Section 4.1.2.1. RFC 8628 Section 3.5 does use it at the token
  endpoint, which weakens that objection.

Should this profile name a code, or stay silent deliberately, so that a client
cannot infer which gate failed?

issues.title: A partial grant has no signal beyond the scope parameter
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
A scope tuple denial narrows the issued token rather than failing the request.
The scope case is covered: RFC 6749 Section 5.1 and RFC 8693 Section 2.2.1
require the `scope` response parameter when the granted scope differs from the
requested scope, and ID-JAG states that granted scopes may be a subset of
those requested.

Nothing covers the rest of it. There is no signal for a narrowed `audience` or
for filtered `authorization_details`, and nothing conveys *why* a privilege
was dropped. A client that asked for three scopes and got two cannot tell
whether the third was refused by policy or was never recognized.

Related to #2, which is the same gap seen from the failure side.

issues.title: Which URN namespace names the capability
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
Section 12.1 sets out three resolutions and leaves the choice to the working
group:

1. This document (or a companion) performs the RFC 3553 registration of the
   `authzen` sub-namespace of `urn:ietf:params`, satisfying the IETF Review
   policy that AuthZEN 1.0 Section 12 asks for and that a specification
   published outside the IETF stream cannot satisfy on its own.
2. Name the capability under `urn:openid:authzen` instead, requesting no IANA
   action. ARAP already does this, so it is the scheme AuthZEN profiles use in
   practice.
3. Decline the dependency and register under `urn:ietf:params:oauth`
   (RFC 6755), whose Specification Required policy is not blocked.

A capability identifier is only useful if both parties compute the same
string, so one scheme for all AuthZEN capabilities is worth more than this
document's independence from any of them. Options 1 and 2 both achieve that
and differ only in which body assigns the name.

Needs to be settled jointly with the AuthZEN WG rather than here alone.

issues.title: Is a new registry the right way to name gate actions?
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
The gate action name is `issue:<token-type>:<grant-type>`, composed from short
names held in two registries this document creates, rather than from the
existing OAuth grant type URIs.

The reason is portability: relation identifiers in real policy engines have
length and character constraints that the URIs exceed, so a composed name
built from URIs could not be carried into a relationship-based engine without
rewriting the policy.

The counter-argument is that inventing a parallel vocabulary for grants that
already have registered identifiers is a cost of its own, and that engines
could canonicalize instead. This is the kind of naming call the working group
is better placed to make.

issues.title: Batch size, latency budget and caching are unspecified
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
A request naming several scopes against several audiences produces a cross
product of evaluations. Section 4.1 addresses colocation and the latency
argument, but the document says nothing about:

- an upper bound on the number of evaluations in one batch, or pagination
- the latency budget an AS should assume on the token path
- whether, and for how long, a decision may be cached

The third is the one with security consequences, since caching a permit is
the thing the whole framework is arguing against doing in a token.

issues.title: Fail closed, but with what response?
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
The draft says that an unreachable PDP, or a malformed decision response,
means the AS fails closed and does not issue. It does not say what the client
sees.

RFC 6749 has no token endpoint equivalent of a 503. HTTP 503 with `Retry-After`
may be sufficient on its own, or `temporarily_unavailable` semantics may need
defining for this endpoint.

This interacts with `I-D.gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response` (cited in
Section 4.2 as the escape hatch for decisions that cannot be made
synchronously): a PDP that is merely slow and a PDP that is down should
probably not look the same to a client.

issues.title: Two smaller questions on the response vocabulary
issues.author: ogazitt
issues.body:
Both carried forward from the analysis that produced Section 6, neither
blocking.

**Refresh token lifetime.** Should `token_lifetime` have a companion key for
the refresh token, or is refresh issuance simply a separate decision with its
own evaluation? The latter is cleaner but means an AS cannot express "issue
this access token, but no refresh token" in a single call.

**Response signing with `crit`.** Should signing the decision response be
REQUIRED when `crit` is used? Leaning no, on the grounds that an attacker who
can strip `crit` can equally flip `decision` to `true`, so `crit` adds no
attack surface that transport security does not already have to cover. A
security area reviewer will ask, so the reasoning should probably be written
down either way.

issues.title: Requested authorization_details are not represented in the evaluation request
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
**Document:** `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-issuance.md` (AuthZEN Profile for OAuth 2.0 Token Issuance). References use heading anchors, since section numbering is generated.

Forming the Evaluation Request (`#request`) surfaces the three request inputs to the PDP three different ways, and `authorization_details` is the odd one out:

- **Scopes**: one scope tuple per requested scope, `action.name` set to the scope value verbatim (Scope Tuple, `#scope-tuple`), decided per item under `execute_all` (Batching and Result Composition, `#composition`).
- **Resource indicators**: the RFC 8707 `resource` (or `audience`) parameter determines a single shared `resource.id` (Resource).
- **`authorization_details`**: no request-side representation. Processing the Evaluation Response (`#shaping`) defines the `authorization_details` constraining key (replace not merge, structural subset per RFC 9396), but nothing carries the *requested* RAR into the evaluation request. The request-construction sections (Subject, Resource, Actions, Context, Batching) never mention it.

**Consequence:** the PDP is required to narrow `authorization_details` and return a subset without ever receiving the requested details in the structured request. They have to be conveyed out of band, which is the shared evaluation-request construction that Related Work (`#related`) already flags as expected alignment work. It is also asymmetric with scopes (which get a real per-item decision), and it is an interop gap, since two PDPs behind one AS have no defined view of the requested RAR.

**Options:**

1. Per-detail tuple, analogous to the scope tuple. One evaluation per requested `authorization_detail`, decided under `execute_all`.
2. Request-side context key carrying the requested `authorization_details` array, so the PDP sees them when computing the shaping key.
3. Status quo, with explicit text that requested `authorization_details` are out of scope of the evaluation request and conveyed by deployment agreement.

A weaker version of the same gap applies to resource indicators: a single `resource.id` on the shared evaluation cannot express multiple requested resources with per-resource narrowing, so `audience` narrows without a per-resource decision.

**Related:** #3 is the response-side counterpart (signalling a partial grant). This issue is the request side, that the PDP never receives the requested `authorization_details` to decide on. Also affects `draft-gazitt-oauth-authzen-token-exchange.md`, which reuses this document's response processing including the `authorization_details` key.
